results.result: Deep mutational scanning (DMS) was successfully performed on VIM-2, generating a high-quality library of ~5600 single amino acid variants. The library was constructed using PCR-based saturation mutagenesis with restriction-free cloning, pooled into seven groups, and subjected to antibiotic selection with ampicillin (AMP), cefotaxime (CTX), and meropenem (MEM) at two temperatures (25°C and 37°C). The library showed excellent coverage (98.7% of variants present) and high replicability between replicates (R² = 0.85-0.94).
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C57 collectively describe the DMS methodology, library construction, selection conditions, and data quality metrics. The experimental design is well-documented with appropriate controls (synonymous and nonsense mutations), multiple replicates, and validation through EC50 measurements (C63-C67). The high R² values between replicates and library coverage statistics provide strong evidence for data quality. The mutation rate estimation (1.4 × 10⁻⁵) from Sanger sequencing supports library quality claims.

results.result: DMS fitness scores were validated against actual antibiotic resistance levels. Synonymous mutations showed near-neutral fitness, nonsense mutations had the lowest fitness scores (centered around -4), and the overall fitness distribution exhibited a bi-modal pattern. EC50 measurements of 45 isolated variants confirmed that fitness scores correlate with resistance levels, with linear correlation ranges identified for each antibiotic and Spearman rank-order correlations ≥0.85.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C67 demonstrate proper validation of the DMS approach. The expected behavior of synonymous (neutral) and nonsense (deleterious) mutations serves as internal controls. The EC50 validation with 45 variants provides independent experimental confirmation of fitness scores. The identification of linear correlation ranges and high Spearman correlations (≥0.85) across all antibiotics strongly supports the reliability of the fitness measurements.

results.result: Global analysis of VIM-2 revealed that 112 positions (42% of residues) are highly sensitive to mutations, with >75% of missense variants showing fitness scores <-2.0. These positions include all six metal-binding residues and are predominantly buried in the protein core (92% with ASA <30%, 63% with ASA <5%). Variants at buried positions (ASA <30%) showed significantly lower fitness than those at exposed positions (P<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C79 describe structural-functional relationships supported by DMS data and structural analysis. The identification of metal-binding residues among highly sensitive positions provides biological validation. The strong association between mutational sensitivity and ASA is supported by both positional analysis and individual variant distributions with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test, P<0.001). The findings are consistent with established protein folding principles cited in C76-C77.

results.result: The distribution of fitness effects (DFE) showed ~65% negative, ~30% neutral, and ~5% positive variants across all antibiotics. A linear model combining ASA, ΔΔG (Rosetta predictions), and wild-type/variant amino acid identity explained 55% of fitness score variation (adjusted R² = 0.55). ASA alone explained 21% of variation, ΔΔG explained an additional 18%, and amino acid identities contributed 10% and 5% respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C91 present a quantitative analysis of fitness determinants. The DFE proportions are consistent with prior DMS studies (C82), providing external validation. The linear modeling approach is appropriate, with clear reporting of variance explained by each predictor. The adjusted R² of 0.55 indicates that structural and biophysical factors explain a majority of fitness variation, though 45% remains unexplained, suggesting additional factors (e.g., dynamics, epistasis) may be important. The statistical approach and model optimization are well-described.

results.result: The VIM-2 signal peptide (residues 1-26) showed distinct mutational tolerance compared to the catalytic domain. Mutations in the signal peptide were generally tolerated (67% neutral, 10% positive), with the DFE significantly more neutral than the catalytic domain (P<0.001). Key findings include: Lys3 is critical for translocation while Lys7 is tolerant to substitution; the hydrophobic region (Val10-Ile16) is most sensitive to charged substitutions; and codon-level fitness dependencies were observed, with 73 of 143 codon-dependent variants occurring in the signal peptide.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C108 characterize signal peptide function through DMS. The findings are supported by appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney U test, P<0.001) and are consistent with established signal peptide biology (citations in C92-C93, C96, C100, C102). The identification of Lys3 as critical while Lys7 is tolerant is supported by both DMS data and natural variant analysis (C101). The codon-level dependencies and mRNA folding energy correlations (C107) are statistically significant and consistent with prior work, though the effect sizes are small (R²=0.06-0.21).

results.result: The signal peptide's less-than-optimal fitness in E. coli may reflect host incompatibility (natural VIM variants are often found in Pseudomonas) or lack of selection for maximum expression in natural environments. The signal peptide is frequently mutated in natural VIM variants, suggesting changes may have facilitated dissemination to different hosts and adaptation to higher antibiotic concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 present speculative interpretations (C109, C110, C112, C113 are explicitly marked as speculation) about why signal peptide fitness is suboptimal. While the observations (frequent mutations in natural variants, C115) are data-supported, the mechanistic explanations remain hypothetical. The claims appropriately cite relevant literature (C111, C112) but lack direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanisms. The inference about dissemination and adaptation (C116) is reasonable but not definitively proven.

results.result: Residues in the catalytic domain were classified into four functional categories: 'tolerant' (55 positions, mostly surface-exposed), 'essential' (20 positions, including all metal-binding residues, deeply buried), 'temperature dependent' (93 positions, mostly buried and hydrophobic), and 'residue dependent' (72 positions, near surface or at packing interfaces). Essential and temperature-dependent residues show enrichment of sidechain-backbone hydrogen bonding and are involved in protein folding and stability, while residue-dependent positions are prominent in active site loops and likely involved in catalysis and substrate interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C132 present a comprehensive functional classification based on DMS data at multiple conditions (temperatures and antibiotic concentrations). The classification criteria are clearly defined (C121) and the structural correlations are well-supported by ASA analysis and hydrogen bonding patterns (C128). The functional interpretations are consistent with structural biology principles and supported by appropriate citations (C128-C129). The distinction between stability-related (essential/temperature-dependent) and catalysis-related (residue-dependent) positions is biologically meaningful and supported by their structural locations.

results.result: Analysis of substrate specificity identified 29 globally positive variants across 10 positions and 78 specificity-altering variants across 25 positions (23/25 near the active site). A strong bias was observed: 96% of specificity variants decreased fitness for AMP and/or CTX, while only three variants decreased MEM fitness. Residues specific to AMP are spread around the active site, while CTX-specific residues are restricted to two active site loops (positions 60-68 and 201-214). Only three variants (R205H/I/V) maintained neutral or higher fitness across all antibiotics.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C155 characterize substrate specificity determinants through systematic comparison of fitness scores across antibiotics. The identification criteria are clearly defined (change in fitness classification plus 2.0 score difference), and specificity was validated by EC50 measurements (C141). The strong bias toward AMP/CTX sensitivity versus MEM is a robust finding supported by multiple lines of evidence. The spatial distribution of specificity residues (C152-C155) is supported by structural analysis and consistent with prior biochemical studies (citations in C153-C155).

results.result: Structural analysis of substrate-residue interactions revealed distinct recognition mechanisms for each antibiotic. AMP interacts with many residues around the active site and is most sensitive to mutations; CTX specificity relies exclusively on active site loop interactions; MEM appears to rely on contacts shared with other antibiotics. Some distant residues affecting AMP specificity do not directly contact substrates, suggesting contributions from solvent-related phenomena or protein dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C163 integrate DMS data with structural analysis using substrate-bound structures from homologous enzymes. The structural observations (C156-C158) are based on appropriate structural alignments. However, the mechanistic explanations for distant residue effects (C159) are explicitly hypothetical and supported only by citations to relevant literature. The overall conclusion about distinct recognition mechanisms (C160-C163) is well-supported by the differential distribution of specificity residues, though the molecular details remain partially speculative.

results.result: Analysis of 56 natural VIM-type variants revealed enrichment for neutral and positive mutations. The fitness distribution showed 31% of globally positive DMS variants are naturally occurring, and 17% of natural mutations have positive fitness for at least one antibiotic. Natural mutations are disfavored in essential (1/20 positions) and temperature-dependent (21/93 positions) residues but common in signal peptide (20/26) and tolerant positions (32/55). Notably, 44% (11/25) of specificity-altering positions have been mutated in natural variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C173 compare DMS data with natural variant sequences, providing evolutionary validation of the experimental findings. The phylogenetic classification into four clades (C165) and identification of 131 unique mutations (C166) are based on appropriate sequence analysis. The enrichment statistics are clearly reported and show strong concordance between experimentally beneficial mutations and natural variation. The observation that specificity positions are frequently mutated (C173) is particularly significant and well-supported by the data.

results.result: Despite overall enrichment for beneficial mutations, 10% of natural mutations are highly deleterious (fitness <-2.0) in the DMS assay. These 13 deleterious mutations across 11 positions are explained by: signal peptide compensatory mutations (K3Q compensated by S6R in VIM-7), substrate specificity changes (Q60H, A143T), global suppression by I185V, and intramolecular epistasis in variants with ≥25 mutations from VIM-2.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C179 address apparent contradictions between DMS predictions and natural variation. The explanations are reasonable and supported by the data: the K3Q/S6R compensation (C176) is directly observable in VIM-7 sequences; the I185V suppressor hypothesis (C178) is supported by its universal presence in natural variants and co-occurrence with otherwise deleterious mutations; and the epistasis explanation (C179) is appropriately invoked for distant variants. However, these remain inferences rather than direct experimental validations of the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: This work reports the first comprehensive mutational analysis of a metallo-β-lactamase (MBL). The study uncovered sensitivity to signal peptide variation potentially due to codon-dependent RNA folding or host translocation system incompatibility, highlighting the importance of genomic and host context in resistance gene compatibility. DMS at multiple conditions enhanced understanding of sequence-structure-function relationships by identifying mutations affecting protein stability, catalysis, and substrate specificity. VIM-2's specificity-altering residues are enriched near the active site, enabling elucidation of enzyme-substrate interaction mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C186 summarize the major contributions of the study. The novelty claim (C182) appears valid as this is the first comprehensive single-amino-acid DMS of an MBL. The findings about signal peptide sensitivity (C183-C184) are well-supported by the data, though mechanistic details remain partially speculative. The characterization of stability, catalysis, and specificity determinants (C185-C186) is strongly supported by the multi-condition DMS approach and represents a significant advance in understanding MBL function.

results.result: The finding that VIM-2's specificity-altering residues are enriched near the active site contrasts with E. coli amidase (amiE), where specificity mutations were distributed across the entire structure. This suggests different enzymes use different mechanisms for substrate recognition, potentially related to structural features: monomeric MBLs have large, solvent-exposed active sites, while amiE has a small, occluded active site and hexameric structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C187-C190 compare the current findings with prior DMS studies, appropriately citing Wrenbeck et al., 2017. The contrast between VIM-2 and amiE is a valid observation supported by both studies. The structural explanation (C189) is reasonable and based on known structural features, though it remains somewhat speculative. The mention of 4-OT (C190) provides additional context showing that quaternary structure alone doesn't determine specificity mechanism. This comparative analysis strengthens the interpretation of the VIM-2 results.

results.result: The study demonstrates that VIM-type variants have continuously evolved by enhancing resistance and altering substrate specificity. The findings suggest potential therapeutic strategies, including combined treatment with carbapenems plus penicillins/cephalosporins to exploit collateral sensitivity, though extensive clinical validation is required. Given the observation of globally positive mutations in natural variants, β-lactams alone are unlikely to be a long-term solution; combination with different antibiotic mechanisms, β-lactamase inhibitors, and surveillance will be necessary. The dataset provides a basis for predicting likely mutations and estimating resistance of future variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C199 discuss implications and future directions. The evolutionary conclusions (C192-C193) are well-supported by the data. However, the therapeutic suggestions (C194-C197) are speculative and appropriately qualified as requiring extensive further investigation. The claim about combined treatment (C194) is based on observed collateral sensitivity patterns but lacks clinical validation. The predictions about future resistance (C198-C199) are reasonable extrapolations but remain to be validated. These claims represent important discussion points but are not directly supported by the experimental data presented.

results.result: Background claims establish that MBLs degrade β-lactam antibiotics and are major sources of multidrug resistance, that resistance genes evolve under antibiotic selection pressure, and that molecular understanding of MBL residue roles (especially in substrate specificity) is lacking despite prior biochemical studies. Deep mutational scanning (DMS) is presented as a method capable of generating comprehensive mutational datasets to address these knowledge gaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C29 and C133-C134 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent the current state of knowledge in the field and appropriately motivate the study. The characterization of DMS capabilities (C24-C29) is supported by citations to prior DMS studies. These background claims are well-established and properly documented.

results.result: The study revealed residues responsible for expression and translocation, mutations that increase resistance and/or alter substrate specificity, and that the distribution of specificity-altering mutations unveiled distinct molecular recognition of three substrates. Function-altering mutations are frequently observed among naturally occurring variants, suggesting continuous evolution toward more potent resistance genes. The study generated comprehensive, high-quality datasets and identified residues critical for VIM-2's function, stability, and substrate specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C11 and C31-C36 summarize the main findings of the study. These summary claims are well-supported by the detailed results presented in other claim groups. The identification of expression/translocation residues (C7) is supported by signal peptide analysis; resistance-increasing and specificity-altering mutations (C8) are documented in the specificity analysis; distinct substrate recognition (C9) is supported by the differential distribution of specificity residues; and the evolutionary conclusions (C10-C11) are supported by natural variant analysis. These represent accurate high-level summaries of supported findings.
